newsitem.title: UK: TABLE TENNIS-WALDNER WIN OVERSHADOWS ADMINISTRATIVE SHAMBLES.
newsitem.headline: TABLE TENNIS-WALDNER WIN OVERSHADOWS ADMINISTRATIVE SHAMBLES.

text.p: Classy Swede Jan-Ove Waldner gave the world table tennis championships a lustre it hardly deserved on Monday with his stirring triumph over young Belarussian Vladimir Samsonov in the men's singles final.
Eight years after he first captured the title, Waldner took it for the second time at the age of 31 and completed a golden run through his seven matches in which he did not drop a single game.
His achievement also banished to the background, the organisational problems that made the championships a nightmare for players and media from the day it began.
Waldner's 21-12 21-17 21-13 victory over a prodigy 10 years his junior was almost the stuff of dreams for a player who could not be blamed if he were starting to plan his retirement party.

His success in the final match of the 12-day tournament meant that China, who won all seven titles at the last championships in 1995, had to settle for six this time, though that was assured on Sunday when Waldner and Samsonov both eliminated Chinese rivals in the semifinals.
But Deng Yaping collected a second straight world women's title to go with her Olympic victory in Atlanta last year and China won all three doubles events along with both team titles.
If only the championships had run as smoothly as Waldner's easy progression to the title. Sadly, it was chaos.

A record 116 countries playing 6,000 matches on 42 tables - the most countries, the most players, the most matches, and the largest collection of results. The information highway would be buzzing non-stop.
The 44th world championships did turn out to be biggest but they were far from being the best.

For a start, a new system for second round group matches in the team event was so complicated no one could understand them. It produced a scheduling nightmare with teams not knowing who and where they were playing two hours before the match.
The public were also affected. Some of those who had bought seats in the main G-Mex arena found them occupied by players.
Consequently, all players and officials were banned from occupying the spectators' stands and those refused included Xu Yinsheng, Chinese president of the International Table Tennis Federation.
A players' strike was then threatened unless the ban was rescinded and the organisers were forced into a swift U-turn to allow them to occupy unreserved seats.
The media suffered when a computerised results system failed to work which meant results often arrived more than two hours after the match was over - or never at all.
Even before the competion was completed, an inquest was underway with ITTF executive vice-president Yapyong Yih of Malaysia placing some of the fault on the shoulders of his own governing body.
"The ITTF should have monitord the situation more closely. It is our responsibility,," he said.
"We should have looked closely at the technical details. We proved too trusting and we were wrong. We are now going to have our own technical director."
Although there had been doubts when Belgrade was re-confirmed as host of the 1999 championships, the Manchester performance provided a fresh perspective.

"The Yugoslavs have good experience of staging world championships and I am sure, no matter what the conditions are, they will provide a better tournament than Manchester," an ITTF official commented.
